# Sea Returns to Drained Fields as Flood Barrier Is Breached

## Coastal council hails largest marsh restoration in the region's history

*By Helen Carteret, Environment Correspondent — 14 June*

The sea flowed back across more than two hundred hectares of farmland on Tuesday
for the first time in three decades, as engineers opened a deliberate breach in
the ageing flood embankment at Saltmere.

The project, the largest of its kind in the region, is intended to recreate the
salt marsh that once lined the estuary before the land was drained for agriculture
in the 1980s. Officials say the restored marsh will absorb storm surge, improve
water quality, and provide habitat for wading birds.

## Mixed feelings among residents

Not everyone welcomed the change. "My grandfather grew barley on that ground,"
said local farmer Tom Reedy, watching the tide creep across the fields. "It is
hard to see it go under. But the floods were getting worse every winter, and the
soil was no good anymore."

Council spokesperson Anita Vohra said the decision followed years of consultation.
"We are not abandoning this land. We are giving it a different job to do, one that
protects the homes behind it."

## What happens next

Monitoring teams will track the return of vegetation and wildlife over the coming
seasons. Early signs are promising: within hours of the breach, gulls and
oystercatchers had already gathered on the newly flooded flats.

The council expects the first salt-marsh grasses to establish within two years.
